title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction
content: A Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) flight physical is a physical examination for "fitness of flight" performed by a physician who is FAA-trained, designated, and certified as an Aviation Medical Examiner (AME), of which there are approximately 2500 in the United States. These physicians are trained to examine and evaluate medical conditions that can cause "sudden incapacitation in flight and/or cause an interruption in the smooth flow of or threat to the safety of our nation's airspace." FAA flight physicals fall into 3 different classes, intuitively designated 1st, 2nd, and 3rd, which are commonly printed/typed in all capital letters. The requirements and valid timeframe for the medical examination depend on the class of medical licensure, the airman's age, and special issuances or other special circumstances. A 1st or 2nd automatically defaults to a 2nd or 3rd after the valid timeframe of the 1st or 2nd. AMEs conduct FAA Medical exams, focusing on exam findings and taking a medical history of factors that may be aeromedically significant. [1] [2] [3]

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction
content: The Human Intervention and Motivational Study (HIMS) is a joint program between the FAA and the aviation industry for initial evaluation, usually followed by ongoing monitoring, wherein there may have been issues with potential concerns about mental health or chemical dependency. HIMS exams and monitoring are weighted more heavily toward history and examination monitoring for sobriety, mental health, drug screening, and correlating reports, such as but not limited to psychiatric, neuropsychological, pilot performance, flight instructor, AA, NA peer-pilots, and chief pilot.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction
content: These examinations are not only performed on pilots but also on ATCs (Air Traffic Controllers) and ASIs (Aviation Safety Inspectors), who may or may not also be pilots. Holding an FAA medical certification is also a standard for a certain degree of overall health. Occasionally, individuals who are not involved in aviation are examined and issued medical certificates. Examples of such persons include workers on offshore oil rigs, where healthcare may be delayed; racecar drivers; and occasionally executives in organizations that cannot afford high rates or unpredictable turnover in certain positions. Student pilots cannot fly solo without an instructor or another pilot until they have passed their medical exam and been issued an FAA medical certificate.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- The Aviation Medical Examiner
content: Any physician (MD/DO) interested in becoming an AME is best suited by having an interest in aviation and an understanding of the concept of a forensic examination, as well as a love of learning and interest in all entities of medicine and capable of performing a comprehensive, thorough medical examination regardless of the Specialty of Origin (SOO). There is no residency training that is not acceptable to become an AME; board certification in the physician's primary specialty is required, and an unrestricted medical license in the state where the FAA medical exams are to be performed. Regardless of SOO, the AME must be thoroughly competent in the ENT, ophthalmologic, neurologic, musculoskeletal, cardiovascular/cardiopulmonary, and psychiatric examination.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- The Aviation Medical Examiner
content: The AME must also be computer-literate, fluent in English, able to adapt to changing regulations/guidelines, and tolerant of a degree of bureaucracy. Fellowships in Aerospace Medicine are available, but few programs have limited positions, and a fellowship is not required for AME certification. [4] The vast majority of AMEs practice medicine full-time and perform flight physicals between patient visits, and the FAA requires only 10 exams per year to maintain certification. 80% of AME's perform less than 25 per year. There are very few AMEs who do nothing more than FAA medicals as their primary job, but many AMEs semi-retire from their SOO and restrict their practice to flight physicals as they scale back toward total retirement. The AME must understand that they are not there to diagnose or treat the airman. While the AME is a doctor, they are not the treating physician, but often speak with the treating physician(s) regarding potential changes to the treatment regimen that could make the difference between issuance of the medical vs. denial or deferral. The AME must understand that they are a representative of the FAA and, by following through, the federal government when interacting with non-AME physicians to assist in the processing of FAA medicals, and that the average non-AME physician most likely does not even know that an FAA AME exists. The AME must recognize clinically significant deterioration in any serious condition requiring urgent or emergent treatment and contact the appropriate treating physician if indicated.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- The Aviation Medical Examiner
content: An AME is often, but not always, required to be a pilot. The AME reports to and is assisted by 1 of 9 Regional Flight Surgeons, who are then responsible to the Federal Air Surgeon (FAS) in Washington DC. The FAS is assisted by Deputy Federal Air Surgeon(s), and there is an additional International "Regional" flight surgeon (RFS). Any AME can contact any RFS or FAS for assistance; this is often helpful after 5 p.m. in the AME's time zone. AMEs are well supported by the RFS and OKC.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- The AME Training and Progression
content: AMEs are initially trained by the Federal Aviation Administration during a 7-day timeframe in Oklahoma City, OK. Advanced practitioners, such as physician assistants and nurse practitioners, are not eligible to serve as AMEs. Currently, there is no plan to authorize physician extenders to certify FAA medicals. This training is a comprehensive, universal review of every specialty and subspecialty from the standpoint of how they pertain to general aviation and the maintenance of health, rather than focusing on direct treatment. This initial training involves what can be an enjoyable, comprehensive review of all medical topics.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- The AME Training and Progression
content: Additionally, training covers aeromedical topics such as decompression, decompression chambers, Time of Useful Consciousness (TOC), evacuation and rescue operations, accident investigation, common patterns of injury, and accident analysis. A static ground-based aircraft is used for simulated emergencies and fake "Hollywood Smoke," as well as the option of another fuselage suspended over a swimming pool, used in training airline attendants in emergency slide use and emergency evacuation into an aquatic environment. The AME trainee is shown how the FAA trains its inspectors, controllers, and administrators. The training also focuses heavily on federal aviation regulations, policies, and procedures for serving as a Federal Government designee. There are several written "open-book quizzes" and a final multiple-choice exam. The exam has a reputation for being difficult but fair, and is well covered in the training course. It does not seem intended to fail or "weed out" AME candidates, but rather to train and prepare them to pass an exam, with the caveat that this material is somewhat esoteric. Very few physicians would pass the exam without taking the course.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- The AME Training and Progression
content: Following initial training and certification, the physician is designated a Junior AME and can perform 2nd and 3rd-class medicals for the next 3 years. During this timeframe, their examination decisions and documentation are evaluated, and the FAA conducts an on-site inspection of the office and equipment. Following this 3-year timeframe, if the error margin is acceptable, the physician may petition to become a Senior AME, examine the airman, and issue 1st-class medicals. At this point, the physician can register to perform physical examinations for ATCs, ASIs, and other FAA employees. AMEs are currently required to complete online training known as MAMERC every 2 years and a 3-day in-person training every 4 years. This training covers a range of topics and focuses heavily on neurology and cardiopulmonary medicine, but it also addresses most major medical topics and guideline updates. The chart of an examined airman may be reviewed periodically. If an AME is contacted, typically via email, the identified errors and any positive or negative feedback may be provided. This training continues throughout the AME's career. This is usually high-quality CME but may not count towards specific requirements in the AME's SOO.

content: The FAA maintains an archive called "FAA TV: AME Minute," a series of short videos covering topics pertinent to AME exams, providing a good review of salient points in training and often explaining guidelines to airmen. Physicians interested in becoming an AME could benefit from reviewing these videos.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- The AME Training and Progression
content: After 3 years as a senior aviation medical examiner, the AME can request training to be designated for the Human Intervention and Motivational Study (HIMS) program and be designated as an Independent Medical Sponsor (IMS) to assist with certification of an airman who has had difficulty with substance abuse, mental health issues, or needs special issuance surrounding antidepressant therapy. [5] Currently, the HIMS AME often works closely with a HIMS psychiatrist or a general psychiatrist familiar with aviation requirements, following a specific template. Additionally, they work with a neuropsychologist designated by the FAA and certified to conduct aviation-specific neuropsychological testing. There are currently only 112 FAA-certified HIMS neuropsychologists worldwide. The AME is also responsible for monitoring the airman, often using a portable breathalyzer; conducting office-based encounters that commonly require 14 random urine drug screens over 12 months; and submitting periodic reports to the FAA before and after the special issuance. The AME is then responsible and held accountable for reporting deviations and concerns to the FAA. There are only 187 HIMS AME's in the US and 20 international HIMS AMEs in 12 other countries at the time of publication.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- "Think Twice" What the AME Candidate Should Know
content: The AME candidate leaves with a clear understanding that they have civil and criminal liability based on their decision(s) beyond medical malpractice. Standard medical malpractice liability does not usually cover forensic examinations.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- "Think Twice" What the AME Candidate Should Know
content: Declining insurance reimbursements and patients' sense of entitlement have led to a burst of "concierge programs," and many new medical school graduates are focused on cash-only business models, such as intravenous fluids and cosmetic procedures. The search for non-insurance-based reimbursement is almost an unfortunate necessity in the modern reimbursement climate. While no doctor is without the potential to be a good AME, the reasons for obtaining this designation should be carefully self-analyzed. Following initial training, the AME is left with an understanding that you are a designee of the federal government. Your superiors are agents of the federal government. Your exams are subject to oversight and evaluation, and your designation may be rescinded based on your documentation, decisions, or failure to meet training and currency requirements. The number of people killed in large commercial airplane crashes rose in 2020. Accident analysis and your role as an AME in prevention are emphasized. While the initial FAA training for AMEs is an outstanding review of nearly every aspect of medicine, portions of the training that cover unpleasant, sad, graphic, and preventable disasters in which the AME was responsible or had the opportunity to prevent the incident are appropriately discussed. At the end of this initial training, the AME candidate leaves with a strong understanding of how serious their responsibility is to airmen, vulnerable passengers, vulnerable people on the ground, the United States, and humanity in general. During training, the question is posed of "How many people can an impaired surgeon kill at a time compared to how many people a 777 can kill based on a single bad decision?" Additional questions addressed what passengers expected and how they felt when fastening their seat belts. The AME candidates were asked to think about the phone calls they made as a passenger on their way to this (the training that day) or any conference to which they took air travel. When the door to the plane was closed, we were asked how much trust and control we had over the situation, and "You were worried about peanuts or chips, not if your pilot was sober, unhealthy, or insane."

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- "Think Twice" What the AME Candidate Should Know
content: The AME needs to complete 1 of 2 3-day courses, one strongly weighted toward neurology and the other strongly weighted toward cardiovascular, every 5 years. Also, to complete online retraining every 2 years. The courses are free for AMEs, funded by taxpayers, and CME credits count toward a regular medical license (Cat 1A). Still, travel and other expenses are the responsibility of the AME, as they are for any other conference.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- "Think Twice" What the AME Candidate Should Know
content: The average pilot is intelligent, dedicated, hardworking, respectful of authority, and usually of a slightly higher socioeconomic and educational status, simply due to the cost requirements and opportunities to enter aviation. The AME should understand the delineation between General Aviation pilots who fly for business, pleasure, and some degree of reimbursement as a flight instructor or persons who have a small airplane and fly mostly on weekends in good weather conditions to things like pancake breakfasts, another type of GA pilot that may have a more technically advanced aircraft with higher performance who flies predominantly for business 250 miles or longer and has additional rating making them able to fly the aircraft purely by reference to flight instruments, and then the truly professional pilot who has achieved the highest rating possible known as the ATP (Airline Transport Pilot) which is often referred to as the "Ph.D. in aviation."

content: ATP are full-time professional aviators whose discipline, focus, and responsibility are comparable to those of cardiothoracic or neurosurgeons at a quaternary care center. Many ATP pilots are highly trained, elite ex-military personnel accustomed to managing high-stakes situations, including the safety of hundreds of passengers on 12- to 14-hour international flights and in challenging weather conditions. AMEs, along with their office staff, must be prepared to interact effectively with a wide range of pilot personalities and to provide professional, efficient service in person, by phone, or via electronic communication.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- MedExpress
content: The FAA maintains a site known as MedExpress. The student pilot is usually introduced and instructed by their flight instructor to set up an initial account that follows the pilot throughout their lifetime. The student pilot or established pilot logs in before the exam and completes the initial entry or updates their current medical history and demographics in the 8500 form. The 8500 form is not unlike the "new patient paperwork" completed when seeing a new primary care provider. They then save or update their information, and a unique code for that exam is generated and is valid for 90 days. They bring this code to the exam, and the AME logs in to the AME's account, enters the code from the pilot or student pilot, and the chart populates. The AME then reviews the history, confirms identity and demographics, and then enters the exam portion of the encounter. This is similar to an EMR, but it lacks an impression or plan section. The AME then submits the completed exam to the FAA electronically, with a status of Issued, Denied, or Deferred for further review. If issued, the AME can print the medical certificate, sign it as the AME, and have the pilot or student pilot sign it. The pilot/student pilot then leaves with the certificate in hand. AMEs are permitted to be "designees," usually staff members who log in and enter demographic data and vital signs, but they cannot enter any other exam information.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- Specifics of the Aviation Medical Exam
content: All exams start with basic demographics, height, weight, body mass index (BMI) calculation, vitals, and a general medical exam of the heart, lungs, and abdomen, along with a basic internal medicine and neuromusculoskeletal annual exam. [6] Scars, tattoos, and any distinguishing body markings must be noted. The exam is documented online by checking normal or abnormal in 24 boxes, in addition to vision and hearing, corresponding to exam items, then providing comments on any abnormalities. Color vision, visual fields, near and distance vision, and optic fundus examination are completed. Heterophoria testing is required for all 1st- and 2nd-class medicals. Intermediate vision is required for 1st- and 2nd-class medicals after age 50. An external anal exam for hemorrhoids is performed, but the digital rectal exam is not required. Females do not require a pelvic exam. Urine dipstick is performed for protein and glucose only, with no drug screen. BMI and obstructive sleep apnea risk are assessed on all airmen, and all airmen are placed into 1 of 6 categories regarding their obstructive sleep apnea status. Hearing requirements for all 3 classes are simply a "conversational speech test" with the AME's back turned to the candidate. ATC requires audiometry at 500, 1000, 2000, 3000, and 4000 Hz. A 12-lead EKG is required only for 1st class medicals, initially at age 35 and then yearly after age 40, and must be transmitted electronically as a PDF. Military flight physicals do not apply to the civilian world and vice versa.

Hearing requirements for all 3 classes are simply a "conversational speech test" with the AME's back turned to the candidate. ATC requires audiometry at 500, 1000, 2000, 3000, and 4000 Hz. A 12-lead EKG is required only for 1st class medicals, initially at age 35 and then yearly after age 40, and must be transmitted electronically as a PDF. Military flight physicals do not apply to the civilian world and vice versa.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- Specifics of the Aviation Medical Exam
content: As a forensic exam, the FFA medical is not covered by insurance, and prices roughly range from $100 to $200 USD. An EKG typically incurs an add-on cost of $25 to $50 USD. Many airlines offer a fixed reimbursement to their airmen who receive 1st-class medicals. With no published reference, it estimates an average of $170 USD for 1st class medical with EKG, $120 USD for 3rd class, and $120 USD for uncomplicated 2nd-class medical. The FAA sets ATC exam pricing at $170 USD for controllers who are federal employees, even though some ATCs are not. FAA employee reimbursement for a new potential ATC candidate with a full audiogram and EKG is $190 USD as of this edit. HIMS programs can range from $ 8,000 to $15,000 over a 1- to 3-year period, with a complex cost breakdown. These numbers vary based on geography.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- Specifics of the Aviation Medical Exam
content: Aeromedical consultation is not an FAA medical examination, but rather a consultative service that may precede an application for an FAA medical certificate or provide guidance toward alternatives such as Sport Pilot privileges or other life pursuits. This consultation is commonly billed at the same rate as a third-class medical. In most cases, within about one hour of the examination and chart or case review, it becomes clear whether the candidate is likely to qualify for a medical and what barriers may exist. However, the AME does not make the final determination. Occasionally, an aeromedical consultation is requested for a minor medical issue, such as a CACI condition, hypertension, or the need for reading glasses. The aeromedicine consult is converted to an FAA medical exam, and a medical may be issued that day.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- Specifics of the Aviation Medical Exam
content: All medical requirements are publicly available in "The Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners," often referred to simply as "the Guide," which can be accessed as a PDF in any web browser. AMEs and individuals assisting airmen in obtaining their medical certificates, such as aviation attorneys and other pilot advocates, need to ensure they have the most recent version of "the Guide," which is continually updated. Another resource for such persons and agencies is the "Federal Air Surgeons Medical Bulletin," a quarterly publication that includes case studies, topics of interest, and proposed or impending changes to federal policy.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Introduction -- The Outcome of the Exam
content: The exam result is either a denial, a deferral, or an issuance. Issuance cases may have restrictions, such as a requirement for vision correction, inapplicability above a certain altitude, inapplicability to night flight, or validity for a period shorter than the class of medical would usually be valid, such as in the case of monitoring. The AME may issue the medical, and the pilot gets a letter from the FAA either requesting additional information or, if the AME made an error, a notice of withdrawal of the medical. It should be noted that the medical certification does not mean the student can fly solo. The instructor or flight school determines when the student can fly solo. A medical certificate is required before flying a plane alone without a co-pilot or instructor. This is referred to as "executing pilot in command privileges."

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Underlying Medical Conditions
content: Most underlying medical conditions are not necessarily disqualifying. Simple osteoarthritis, the need for near-vision correction, and various underlying medical conditions may qualify outright, require Conditions AME's Can Issue, or require special issuance. [7] Seldom is a medical denied outright. Noting that issuance of a medical requires that the airmen "May reasonably be expected, for the maximum duration of the airman medical certificate applied for or held, to make the person unable to perform those duties or exercise those privileges" means that entities such as terminal metastatic disease, rapidly progressive multiple sclerosis, or structural cervical stenosis with myelopathy would be denial cases. Denial by the AME is discouraged by the FAA and requires an additional letter to the FAA. Deferrals are common in many medical conditions, such as coronary artery disease. The candidate typically receives follow-up correspondence from the FAA, usually a certified letter, following the deferral that outlines what else is required for review, such as hospital records, labs, stress tests, and an echocardiogram (EKG), commonly with a 60- to 90-day deadline. It is not uncommon for several reviews and requests to go back and forth with the FAA, which may request additional information during the ongoing review. The AME must be tolerant of this process and able to explain and counsel the candidate throughout it. It is not uncommon to request an extension to the deadline. If the FAA does not respond to the request, the medical is invalidated or denied outright for "failure to provide."

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Special Issuance
content: There are 15 FAA "Disqualifying Conditions"; however, in many cases, when the condition is adequately controlled, the FAA issues medical certification contingent on periodic reports. This is known as a Special Issuance. The AME is responsible for the actual exam and makes the deferral. The FAA issues its requirements, and the AME may or may not assist with the FAA's response. The FAA then issues a special issuance or denies outright based on the information it receives. In the case of the special issuance, the FAA issues the medical certificate, which bears the signature of a regional flight surgeon. The initial special-issuance insurance outlines the AME's responsibilities for subsequent medical issuances during the special issuance. A 1st class special issuance for CAD through a senior AME or a special issuance through a HIMS AME for a history of more than 1 episode of driving under the influence are both examples of special issuance. The initial letter from the FAA for a special issuance clearly outlines what must be completed at the time of the repeat special issuance, including required reports from counselors or peer pilots and documentation such as EKG and stress test results. It also specifies the validity period, typically 6 months or 1 year, rather than the standard duration of the class medical. The special issuance usually does not revert to a lower class of medical certificate once the designated special issuance timeframe has elapsed. A 1st-class medical issued for CAD often includes the restriction: "not valid for any class after 6 months." The AME then follows the FAA outline and is responsible for communicating deterioration in the special issuance condition; they are liable outside of medical malpractice if they fail to do so.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Conditions AMEs Can Issue
content: Conditions AMEs can issue (CACI) is a set of conditions that allows AMEs to issue, without back-and-forth correspondence with the FAA, a determination of whether the applicant meets the parameters of a CACI Condition Worksheet. There are currently 19 CACI conditions listed in "the Guide." These are not disqualifying conditions; examples include stable, retained nephrolithiasis, controlled hypertension, or hypothyroidism. The worksheets provide detailed instructions to the examiner and outline condition-specific requirements for the applicant. [8] This is not the same as a special issuance. If all the CACI criteria are met and the applicant is otherwise qualified, the AME may issue it on the 1st exam or the 1st time the condition is reported to the AME without contacting AMCD/RFS. Document the appropriate notes in Block 60 of the 8500 and retain the supporting documents with the AME. They do not need to be submitted to the FAA at the time of issuance but must be maintained in the AME's file. If the requirements are not met, the AME must defer the exam and send the supporting documents to the FAA. If an astute physician reviewed the guidelines on the condition flowsheets, they would likely find that these are very reasonable, up-to-date medical guidelines that comply with the standard of care in the relevant specialty.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Medication Use
content: The FAA maintains a list of acceptable medications, all of which require monitoring. Certain medications in combination are not permitted, and certain meds, such as clonidine, are not permitted for chronic use of any controlled substances. [9] Insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus is an absolute contraindication for a 1st class medical due to the risk of hypoglycemia, but an IDDM may potentially qualify for 2nd or 3rd class medicals with an initial special issuance. Medications that can cause drowsiness are the most common drugs found in a deceased pilot at autopsy in the FAA's report on incidental autopsy findings produced in September 2018. These medications are permitted after 6 half-lives; the list of approved medications is available in the Air Force Aerospace Medicine Approved Medications list. The most common drug found at autopsy is diphenhydramine.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Acute vs. Chronic Conditions
content: Acute issues such as upper respiratory infection and orthopedic fractures are the airman's responsibility to ground themselves until they are healthy and recovered. Many airlines have their own policy on returning acutely ill/injured pilots to active flight status. An airman who needs an elective procedure, such as cosmetic surgery or a colonoscopy, may return to flight status once fully recovered and off all medications, including pain medications. Pilots may consult their AME regarding return-to-flight status. Airlines often have their own guidelines on these return-to-cockpit timelines.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Pregnancy
content: The FAA provides minimal specific guidance regarding medical certification and pregnancy, instead deferring decision-making to the patient and her obstetrician. Under normal circumstances, pregnancy is not disqualifying, and air travel during pregnancy is generally considered safe. [10] [11] Applicants are advised to inform their obstetrician of all aviation-related activities to ensure individualized guidance. The Aviation Medical Examiner may choose to counsel applicants about the risks and practical considerations of piloting an aircraft during the third trimester. For a variety of safety and liability reasons, few flight instructors knowingly conduct flight training with pregnant students. It is important to note that pregnant flight students and pilots may continue to take and pass ground examinations and maintain proficiency using flight simulators until the period of confinement has ended and recovery from pregnancy is complete.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Statement of Demonstrated Ability (SODA)
content: The FAA issues a SODA as an option for an airman with a "static non-progressive defect" to have an opportunity to demonstrate that their impairment is not AERO-medically significant. A SODA is often issued after a "Medical Flight Exam." The most common SODA is issued for color vision deficiency, in which a local FAA representative observes a pilot identifying red, white, and green light gun signals from an air traffic control tower. [12] This may or may not require a flight. Other examples include monocular vision and an amputated limb, with or without a prosthetic limb, which may require that the limb be worn while exercising pilot-in-command privileges. The AME does not perform the Medical Flight Exam; instead, a designated pilot examiner or safety officer from the FAA who is clearly capable of safely flying the aircraft used in the Medical Flight Exam. The SODA does not need to be repeated with each medical exam, and airmen with SODA have it for life. The number must be entered and documented on all subsequent medical exams. There have indeed been several "interesting" medical flight exams in the FAA's history.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Equipment List
content: The FAA requires a minimum equipment list that the AME must maintain in their office. These include simple things such as a sphygmomanometer, stethoscope, otoscope, ophthalmoscope, and Snellen eye chart. There are alternatives to visual field, conjugate gaze, and color vision testing. There are many "either-or" options and a list of several different types of vision tests that are acceptable. The FAA issues a mandatory standard near- and intermediate-vision card, prepaid envelopes for special issuance, and CACI documents upon request.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Aircraft and Phase Considerations
content: The class of medical examination may also be related to the aircraft being flown. The 3rd-class medical permits a pilot to fly any aircraft with a gross weight of less than 12,500 pounds (5670 kg) and fewer than 3 engines. Any flying that is done for hire, such as transporting passengers or paid cargo, requires 2ne or 1st class certification, plus there are other requirements, such as a commercial rating, in addition to endorsements such as pressurized endorsement, and instrument rating, which is beyond the scope of this topic but is mentioned because they should not be confused with medical class requirements. [13] The medical certification alone does not qualify the pilot to fly any particular aircraft.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Aircraft and Phase Considerations
content: The initial rating a pilot earns is the Private Pilot License (PPL), and the training consists of 2 phases. Initially, a student pilot flies with an instructor. Then the student flies solo and is not allowed to have anyone else in the aircraft, including an instructor or another pilot who is not an instructor; in that case, the student is merely a passenger. Eventually, the student passes their written and practical exams and earns their PPL, at which point they are then allowed to take passengers. During the initial phase of training with the instructor, the student is typically required to undergo a medical exam. The medical exam is required before the 1st solo flight. Some aeronautical institutions, flight schools, colleges, and even private flight instructors require a medical exam before accepting a student and investing time and energy in them. Additionally, financial aid programs may require passing the medical before considering funding aviation education.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Aircraft and Phase Considerations
content: Much like a driver needs car insurance, pilots need aircraft insurance for personally owned aircraft. If hangered at an airport, the airport usually requires it to be listed as "additionally insured." This is relevant because recent trends in insurance aviation have, in some cases, exceeded FAA requirements. There are currently no aviation insurance companies that insure a pilot over 70 in any aircraft with retractable gear, regardless of a 1st-class medical. Some insurance companies may not accept "Basic Med," discussed later, for "complex high performance" (defined as an engine greater than 200 brake HP at sea level, flaps, a variable-pitch propeller, and retractable landing gear). They may even mandate an exam every 6 months for insurance purposes. While the medical may be valid for 2 years, the airman must visit the AME and recertify to remain insured. Note that insurance is not a legal requirement. Many private airstrips and pilots are uninsured and may not be permitted to land at certain airports as a result.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- Monocular Contacts
content: This topic warrants mention because it has been a persistent source of confusion and accidents. Many people wear a contact lens in their non-dominant eye for near-vision correction, allowing them to avoid reading glasses. There is a specific question on the 8500 form: "Do you wear near-vision contact lenses when flying?" While this may be convenient for the average middle-aged person in their day-to-day life, it impairs depth perception, especially at relatively high speeds, and is thus an absolute no for FAA medical certification. Such persons often end up with a restriction on their medical certificate stating "Must have near vision correction available," and then wear low-profile "readers." Similar to driving a car, the pilot looks out the cockpit window and down through the cockpit to read items on their lap, such as maps and checklists. There are anecdotal reports of "teams" or couples who often fly together, where 1 has near vision, and the other does not. The pilot in command is a single person who must be able to manage all aspects of flight and operate the aircraft independently. This includes reading instruments at intermediate distance, reading charts at near distance, and looking outside the aircraft for distant vision. This should be differentiated from planes that require 2 pilots, often pilot in command and 2nd in command, or more complicated aircraft that require other crew, such as navigators, flight engineers who may need nothing other than near vision, but still need to hold a medical certificate.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- "Basic Med": a non-FAA 3rd class Substitute
content: Technically, "Basic Med" is not an FAA or AME topic, but it is relevant to aviation medicine and AME practice. In addition to issuing a follow-up 3rd-class medical to an airman, with or without a special issuance, there is an option known as BM (Basic Med). Airmen requiring 1st- or 2nd-class medicals are NOT able to exercise those privileges under basic med.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- "Basic Med": a non-FAA 3rd class Substitute
content: This is a relatively recent program under which any medical doctor, including an AME, can examine the patient, complete the paperwork, sign it, and the airman can fly as if they had a 3rd-class medical. The airman must complete an online course every 2 years and be evaluated by an MD/DO every 4 years. Two caveats are that they must have had a previously valid 3rd-class medical and that their most recent medical must not have been denied, deferred, or revoked. Again, this is only the 3rd class, and it occurs only after an initial certification by an AME. Pilots cannot do Basic Med as initial certification. There may be other factors to consider, such as aircraft liability insurers that routinely require information on the pilot's continued training, certification, and medical status, as well as the aircraft's condition. It may substantially increase rates if the pilot is flying under Basic Med. Many doctors pause when they look at the paperwork and the attestation they are asked to sign. Medical Mal insurance carriers were known to send policy clarifications to insured physicians; they are not covered for Basic Med. Likewise, many hospital systems and large groups have made it clear they do not provide that service and recommend/refer to an AME. When redone annually for stable disease, special issuances often require additional testing and labs that may not be covered by health insurance. Such cases are often simplified by getting Basic Med. Pilots who require a 1st- or 2nd-class medical based on their job or the type of aircraft they fly are not eligible.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Issues of Concern -- "Basic Med": a non-FAA 3rd class Substitute
content: Issues have arisen, and it is not uncommon for pilots who attempted to obtain a medical, had it deferred or denied, then went to a non-AME and had the paperwork completed. While they may have the paperwork in hand, it is not valid. Furthermore, the course clearly covers when the Basic Med is valid and when it is not, and it concludes with an attestation to that effect. Pilots ignoring this or saying they "didn't know" when they had to pass a quiz about under what circumstances Basic Med is not valid as a defense in front of the NTSB, their insurance carrier, or any of several regulatory agencies.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Clinical Significance
content: Most healthcare professionals are unaware that a pilot needs a separate medical certification from an FAA-designated AME or that an AME even exists. There are cases of mid-level practitioners or other non-physicians writing something to the effect of "OK to fly the airplane" on a prescription pad or return-to-work slip, and the student pilot then brings this to their flight instructor, thinking it is a valid "Flight Physical." There are cases of candidates being confused and setting up and taking Department of Transportation (DOT) exams, thinking they are the same.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Clinical Significance
content: It is important to understand the difference between a clinical exam and a forensic exam. Similar to an Independent Medical Exam for Workers' Comp or Personal Injury, an FAA flight physical for a civilian, military/government pilot, or an air traffic controller is not a clinical medical exam but rather a forensic examination. No diagnosis is made, and no treatment is rendered. As always, during the examination, clinical concerns may arise that the physician must report and/or render emergent treatment deemed necessary to avoid further injury or impairment, such as noting melanoma, a diastolic murmur, severe edema, or an abnormal EKG.

title: Pilot Medical Certification -- Clinical Significance
content: With such regular follow-up and strict guidelines, pilots, even those with underlying diseases, usually receive care and follow-up they might not otherwise receive. Many take better care of themselves and are more mindful of their health to enjoy the hobby of flying or pursue their profession.
